title: Bored at Work You May Be Feeling 'Rustout'
paragraphs: Most people have heard of burnout, the exhaustion that comes from too much stress at work. But researchers are paying growing attention to a less obvious problem known as "rustout."

Rustout describes a gradual loss of energy and motivation that occurs when a person's abilities are not being used in meaningful ways. While burnout is caused by too much pressure and too little recovery, rustout is caused by too little challenge, stimulation and growth. In other words, people can suffer not only from having too much to do, but also from having too little that engages them.

People experiencing rustout often feel underused, stuck or intellectually stagnant. They may continue to meet their targets, but without any real sense of investment, and some begin to consider leaving their jobs. Because the process is slow and quiet, it is easy for colleagues and managers to miss.

A recent study by Sabrina Fitzsimons, a lecturer at Dublin City University in Ireland, and David S. Smith explored the problem among teacher educators. Although most participants said they enjoyed their work, the researchers found an undercurrent of experiences that pointed to rustout.

The researchers identified several causes. These include heavy administrative workloads that push out the parts of the job people value most, reduced independence, and a mismatch between people's goals and the tasks they are given. Ironically, reliable and hard-working employees may be at particular risk, because they are often given more of the same work instead of new challenges. Rustout is not limited to older workers; it can also appear in the middle of a career.

The American Psychological Association has also noted that rustout is often less about personal boredom and more about how work is designed. It cited a study linking higher levels of job boredom to reduced heart rate variability, a measure of how well the nervous system is functioning.

So what can be done? Experts suggest that individuals ask themselves whether they feel fulfilled and able to use their talents, and then discuss these questions with their managers. Organizations, meanwhile, can offer dependable employees opportunities for development.
